Research taste in particular may be trickier than it looks. Say the next generation of AI really does have an interesting, high-taste set of research directions to pursue. Well presumably find those fast, after which the fruit will have been plucked, and the ideas will no longer be high taste (because they’ve been explored en masse). This is a similar dynamic to the ever-moving target of “slop.” *Any* output that is recognizably of the agents becomes slop, or at least commodified, in a sense, once that output is sufficiently promulgated in bulk. Certain styles of math paper will become (are becoming) slop. Certain styles of web design already are. On and on it will go. It’s unclear if any kind of media/intellectual output proliferated at such scale can remain high taste, even if we’d have considered it genius from a human just a few years ago.

The bar will continually be raised. The world will get smarter as what was once brilliance becomes commodified, but *what was once brilliance will nevertheless be commodified.* And so the definition of brilliant will change. The wedge for continued value creation by humans lies here, I would guess.

Recently there was a story reporting on OpenAI’s form 5500 (the public disclosure about our 401k program) which some people used to make observations with the flavor of “see, they don’t REALLY believe in advanced AI, or else they wouldn’t be saving money!”

I contribute to my openai-sponsored 401k as well as other conventional retirement-savings vehicles. I cannot speak for any of my colleagues, but I can tell you why I personally make these contributions.

First there is the reality that the whole “advanced AI means money has no value, either because we live in utopia and everything’s free or because we are all dead” are extreme ends of the spectrum of possible futures. It is true that things of this flavor, or other scenarios similar enough to this that one’s retirement savings don’t matter, *are* possible outcomes. But also there are many other plausible transformative futures, and I’m enough of a Burkean that I’m not going to jettison some of the oldest financial wisdom humans have developed (save money!) over my own projections about the future. It wouldn’t be responsible to my family, for one thing.

Family is an important part of my thinking on this topic for other reasons. In some sense, I want to live in a future where having set aside money for retirement is still prudent. That would mean the future, however transformed, is still familiar enough. A world where it truly doesn’t matter whether uou save may be a lovely place to live (or it may not), but regardless of its desirability it is a world SO transformed that, again, my Burkean prior kicks in. 

I *hope* the future is at least vaguely familiar to me as I exist today. I hope that at least some of the habits I have learned still matter in that future, and that some of the wisdom I have learned holds true. I hope that not just for me but for my son and future children. I do a lot of things out of this hope, and one small example is that I contribute to a 401k. 

A lot of people made their sneering observations about OAI employees’ 401k contributions, saying “derp de doo, revealed preferences, they don’t believe what they say.” That’s fine. Maybe that IS why some frontier AI company staff save for retirement. But I’d characterize my mentality about savings more as an article of faith at this point, and my biweekly 401k contributions as tiny prayers for a vaguely recognizable future.

To be quite frank, a lot (not all!) of these “rogue agent hacks” on government statistical websites are things that think-tank interns and research assistants have done for many years. I have known many a think tank paper that was enriched by an enterprising RA using eg urlquery to find CSVs and PDFs on government agency websites that were publicly accessible and non-sensitive but nonetheless not things the agency *intended* to be on their website. Is it “hacking” to find those things? Is it hacking in the even more innocuous examples where agents are literally just accessing tabular data available on a government statistical website, just a version of that data that is easier to access and analyze programmatically? 

This constant trickle of examples (which tbc I have personally seen many models do, before I joined OpenAI; it is even something I have discussed with models before!) will probably have the effect of diminishing the importance of “an AI hack” on the eyes of the observing public by creating an oversupply of “AI hack” examples. I am a fan of the cyberpunk aesthetics of bringing back old technological concepts to solve distinctly present-day problems. In this case, Apple’s new anti-deepfake tech brings back the language of film in a non-cheesy way. Essentially the phone camera sensor cryptographically signs each pixel of a digital “negative,” which is then “developed” in the cloud with all of Apple’s image processing steps. This makes the processing legible and auditable (unlike on-device processing, which can be corrupted with or without the user’s knowledge).

This strikes me as especially useful in the context of the judicial system, where I have long worried that AI-manipulated media could gum up the works (see attached excerpt from the AI Action Plan). Allowing forensic experts to inspect the image processing in Apple’s secure cloud seems better suited to proceedings where the truth of evidence *really* matters. 

There are of course many ways in which Apple has not done a good job keeping up with the AI era, but this is a cool example of them doing thoughtful work.
